narrative.text: The cover page of the 2021 WHO global guidance on criteria and processes for validating elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B virus.
A blank page with no text.
The inner title page of the 2021 global guidance on validating elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B.
The copyright and cataloguing page of the 2021 EMTCT validation guidance, noting it updates the 2017 edition and giving ISBNs, licence terms and disclaimers.
The table of contents of the EMTCT validation guidance, listing chapters on rationale, indicators and targets, validation processes and annexes on measuring HBV indicators.

A foreword recounting the history of global efforts to validate elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis since 2014, including Cuba's validation in 2015. It stresses human rights and the involvement of women living with HIV or HBV in services.

Continuation of the foreword, explaining that this third version sets standard criteria for validating triple elimination and recognising high-burden countries on the Path to Elimination, signed by the WHO HIV, hepatitis and STI programmes director.

Acknowledges the WHO programmes, Global Validation Advisory Committee members and others who developed the guidance, describing how the third version was produced through virtual meetings and consultation.
Continues the acknowledgements, naming regional EMTCT focal points and WHO staff and noting PEPFAR funding through CDC and USAID.
Lists essential WHO web resources on triple elimination, validation processes, regional websites and related guidance.
A list of abbreviations and acronyms used in the guidance.
Glossary entries taken from WHO guidelines, defining terms such as adequate syphilis treatment, early infant diagnosis and informed consent.
Further glossary definitions, covering terms such as integrated service delivery, integration, quality assurance and quality control.
The final glossary entries, defining terms such as quality management system, rapid diagnostic test, testing algorithm and validation.

Opens the executive summary by describing the global commitment to eliminate vertical transmission of HIV, syphilis and HBV and the purpose of the goal. It cites 2030 targets including zero new infant HIV infections and HBsAg prevalence of 0.1% or less in young children.

Recounts the development of the EMTCT validation guidance from the 2014 "Orange Book" through later editions, with requirements in data, laboratory, programme and human rights areas. It introduces a summary table of targets.

A table summarising impact and programme targets for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and HBV, from 2030 global targets to specific validation thresholds, with explanatory footnotes.

Lists the changes in the third version of the guidance, such as adding HBV validation criteria and Path to Elimination recognition, revising laboratory quality standards and expanding guidance on low-performing subnational units. It ends by expressing WHO's hope that the guidance will speed progress.

Describes the contribution of vertical transmission to the HIV epidemic, with UNAIDS estimates of new child infections in 2020 compared with the 2000 peak. It notes that the guidance also applies to trans and gender diverse people who can become pregnant.
Lists key interventions for preventing vertical HIV transmission, then describes the burden of congenital syphilis and of HBV, noting that most chronic HBV infections are acquired in childhood.

Notes WHO's recommendation for hepatitis B birth dose and infant vaccination, then explains how elimination of vertical transmission is defined and validated as a public health problem. It also describes regional frameworks for triple elimination, such as in the Western Pacific.

Defines validation as confirmation that a country has met EMTCT criteria while protecting human rights and involving women living with HIV or HBV. It outlines the history of earlier editions of the guidance.
A box summarising what is new in the third version, including HBV criteria, laboratory standards and subnational selection, and describing the Path to Elimination category for high-burden countries.
Recaps revisions made in the second edition and explains that the third version adds HBV for triple elimination, noting Botswana as the first country recognised on the Path to Elimination.

Sets out the qualifying requirements countries should meet before applying for validation, including national-level evidence of meeting targets, and recommends a preliminary self-assessment checklist.

Continues the qualifying requirements, covering surveillance systems able to detect most vertical infections, meeting criteria in the lowest-performing subnational unit, and programme, human rights and community engagement requirements.

Explains the epidemiological and programme considerations behind the validation criteria, such as frequent asymptomatic infection, the importance of testing and treatment in pregnancy, infant HBV vaccination and protection of women's rights.
A table of country options for single, dual or triple validation, with a note that countries should report data on all three infections even if seeking single or dual validation.
A box summarising the impact and process targets required for global validation of EMTCT of HIV, syphilis and HBV, such as MTCT rates, case rates and HBsAg prevalence thresholds.
Sets out the two impact targets for validating EMTCT of HIV, an MTCT rate below 5% or 2% and 50 or fewer paediatric cases per 100 000 live births, and describes recommended infant testing schedules.
Explains the HIV MTCT rate and how it relates to the case rate, giving a formula for calculating the case rate from maternal prevalence and MTCT rate.

A box on the rationale for using a case rate of new paediatric HIV infections, listing its advantages for comparability and for reflecting prevention efforts. It notes that process indicators should cover all pregnant women living with HIV, including migrants and key populations.

Lists limitations of HIV vertical transmission and case rates drawn from studies and household surveys, such as missing women outside PMTCT programmes, maternal seroconversion during pregnancy or breastfeeding, early child deaths and loss to follow-up. It recommends modelled estimates as a remedy, noting their weaker reliability in low-prevalence concentrated epidemics, and begins explaining how the Spectrum model accounts for breastfeeding duration and maternal treatment timing.

Explains that Spectrum model estimates capture child HIV infections at population level, including among women outside programmes and those who seroconvert, but depend heavily on accurate data on pregnant women on and retained on ART. It then introduces the surveillance case definition for congenital syphilis, covering stillbirths and live births to inadequately treated seropositive mothers and children with clinical or laboratory evidence of infection.

Sets out why congenital syphilis is underreported, including limited laboratory and radiographic testing, unrecognized stillbirths and subtle clinical signs that require skilled providers. It explains the reasoning behind the surveillance case definition and the 2015 expert decision to use live births as the denominator, matching the HIV case rate.

Lists the laboratory and radiographic findings consistent with congenital syphilis, from detection of Treponema pallidum and abnormal cerebrospinal fluid results to suggestive long-bone X-rays and infant serology titres compared with the mother's. It then introduces the WHO Congenital Syphilis Estimation Tool for estimating case rates and planning treatment scale-up where data are poor.

Presents a figure on the main strengths of the WHO Congenital Syphilis Estimation Tool, such as estimating case rates and the benzathine penicillin needed. A box on managing maternal syphilis cites WHO screening and treatment guidance, defines adequate treatment and advises when to evaluate women for reinfection.

Introduces the impact indicators for validating elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B, aimed at preventing or minimizing vertical transmission. Countries with universal timely birth-dose vaccination must show HBsAg prevalence of 0.1% or less among children aged five and under, while those using a targeted birth dose must also show a transmission rate of 2% or less.

Explains the rationale for using HBsAg prevalence of 0.1% or less in young children as the hepatitis B impact target, since most chronic infections come from perinatal transmission and child prevalence is a proxy for incidence. It allows flexibility in age groups for serosurveys and notes that infants under nine months should not be tested because maternal antibodies cause false negatives.

Explains the additional 2% hepatitis B transmission-rate target for countries using a targeted birth dose or with high-prevalence subpopulations, defining how the rate is calculated. It then introduces process indicators, requiring at least 95% coverage of first antenatal visits and of HIV and syphilis testing among pregnant women for at least two years.

Gives the rationale for near-universal HIV and syphilis testing in early pregnancy and for using pregnant women attending antenatal care as the denominator for syphilis testing coverage. It also covers lifelong ART for all women living with HIV and the 95% target for adequate treatment of syphilis-seropositive pregnant women.

Explains that syphilis treatment with benzathine penicillin at least 30 days before delivery is needed to prevent infant infection and mentions dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests. It lists the hepatitis B programme targets, including 90% coverage of infant vaccination, timely birth dose, antenatal HBsAg testing and antivirals for high-viral-load mothers.

Sets out the rationale for hepatitis B programme targets, linking them to the global health sector strategy goals for vaccination, diagnosis and treatment. It explains that 90% coverage of the third infant dose and timely birth dose is expected to achieve the impact targets, and that high antenatal testing coverage matters mainly where the birth dose is targeted.

Explains why the 90% antiviral coverage target for eligible HBsAg-positive pregnant women is lower than ART and syphilis treatment targets, as vaccination is the main tool against hepatitis B transmission. It also advises countries to monitor follow-up of exposed infants and notes that regions may add their own non-mandatory indicators.

Opens the chapter on foundational requirements for validation, stating that elimination requires quality diagnostics, prevention and treatment services, strong health information systems and respect for human rights, gender equality and community engagement. It begins the data system requirements, such as capturing public and non-public sector data, using standard case definitions and protecting privacy.

Continues the data requirements, calling for subnational and subpopulation disaggregation and country assessment of data completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness with a dedicated verification tool. It then turns to laboratory quality, citing ISO 15189 standards and listing key requirements such as quality management, testing algorithms, quality control and external quality assessment.

Sets out what laboratories contributing surveillance and monitoring data must have, namely quality management systems, quality-assured test kits, trained staff and routine quality assurance with external assessment. It describes how the laboratory assessment reviews national testing algorithms and the suitability of the tests chosen.

Describes the remaining laboratory assessment areas, staff competence and laboratory data management, including timely return of results. It then outlines the programme assessment, which reviews national policies and guidelines, services in public and non-public sectors and the performance of low-coverage areas and subpopulations.

Requires countries to show that services reach even the lowest-performing subnational units and least-served subpopulations. It introduces the requirement that programmes respect international standards on human rights, gender equality and community engagement, and lists assessment steps such as stakeholder interviews and consultations with women using services.

Notes that leaving no one behind and health equity are central to WHO strategies and that the hepatitis B component also adopts human rights, gender and community principles. It describes governments' obligations to respect, protect and fulfil rights, including sexual and reproductive health and rights, in preventing vertical transmission.

Explains how gender inequality and harmful norms can limit women's access to services and autonomy, making gender equality critical to preventing vertical transmission. It describes the assessment tool's markers and its three guiding questions on human rights, gender equality and meaningful engagement of affected women.

Explains that the qualitative assessment requires consultations with stakeholders, especially women who use the services and their networks, who can identify barriers and solutions. It states that assessors must have relevant expertise and involve people from networks of women with HIV alongside experts in human rights and gender.

A table setting out the key steps, roles and responsible bodies for the human rights, gender equality and community engagement component of validation, from involving networks of women living with HIV and hepatitis B to holding a dialogue on findings and giving feedback.

Explains that many sub-Saharan African countries cannot reach validation thresholds because high maternal HIV or syphilis prevalence keeps child case rates high even with low transmission rates. It opens the chapter on the path to elimination and lists the prevalence levels that make a country eligible to apply.

States that countries seeking certification on the path to elimination follow the same procedure as for validation. It begins a table of prevalence requirements, impact indicators and programme targets for each tier, with the bronze-tier targets for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B.

Continues the tier table with silver and gold requirements, such as transmission rates below 2% or 5% and paediatric case rates of 250 or fewer per 100,000 live births for the gold tier. It explains that moving up tiers brings a country closer to elimination and that the same principles apply to hepatitis B.

A table of scenarios linking antenatal HIV prevalence and a transmission rate below 5% to expected infant case rates and the applicable gold, silver or bronze tier, contrasted with full validation thresholds. It then begins describing why many countries face a high hepatitis B burden, including low birth-dose coverage and limited diagnostics.

Explains the rationale for the hepatitis B path-to-elimination tiers, with bronze recognizing a universal timely birth-dose policy and higher tiers reflecting coverage milestones. It notes that hepatitis B path-to-elimination recognition is granted only at regional level unless the region asks for global recognition.

Opens the chapter on special populations and circumstances, noting that migrants, displaced people, indigenous people, adolescent girls and other vulnerable groups may face higher risk and poorer access to antenatal care. It also asks validation reports to describe the infant feeding choices and counselling offered to women living with HIV.

Specifies infant HIV testing at 6–8 weeks and 18 months, or three months after breastfeeding ends, so that all infections are captured, including in non-breastfeeding settings. It introduces special considerations for small countries and island states, whose data should be verified by regional structures during country missions.

Explains that regional and global committees may remove from the numerator infant cases judged not to be programme failures, after reviewing individual case reports. It asks countries with small numbers to provide case studies of exposed infants while preserving anonymity.

A table showing how annual and four-year pooled HIV transmission and infant case rates vary in small countries with few pregnant women or cases. It adds that small countries may use the 2% hepatitis B transmission target, which requires high antenatal testing coverage.

Explains that PMTCT services provided by private, nongovernmental, faith-based and other non-public bodies should be included in national monitoring and reported together with public data. It adds that the programme assessment should compare access, delivery and payment in the non-public sector with the public sector.

Opens the chapter on the validation process, emphasizing a public health approach that strengthens health systems while upholding rights, participation and gender equality. It advises countries to confirm they meet minimum criteria before applying and describes the national, regional and global teams that verify country reports using standard assessment tools.

Describes guiding principles and partners in validation, including UN agencies such as UNAIDS, UNICEF and UNFPA, with the health ministry initiating the process. It begins the national-level steps, starting with the ministry's formal request letter sent through the WHO country office.

Lists further validation steps, including establishing a national validation committee, completing a preliminary assessment checklist and preparing the national report. It then describes regional review and the global review by the Global Validation Advisory Committee, which advises WHO whether the country should be validated or certified.

Describes the final step, in which the WHO Director-General signs a validation certificate sent with follow-up recommendations through the Regional Office. A figure summarizes the full validation and certification process and the responsibilities at national, regional and global levels.

Opens the chapter on maintaining validation, explaining that sustained elimination needs monitoring and surveillance that track coverage and detect most cases, including in vulnerable groups. A table sets out the time intervals for maintenance reviews by country type and number of infections validated.

Describes how countries apply for maintenance of validation, with the global secretariat keeping the list of validated countries and scheduling reviews. Countries prepare reports using a template and should describe programme changes or disruptions, such as those caused by COVID-19 or natural disasters.

Describes what countries must submit when reporting on maintaining validation of elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, and how regional committees review these reports before passing them to the global secretariat. It also explains that after two global maintenance reviews, countries that keep meeting targets may be transferred to regional review, following a vote of the Global Validation Advisory Committee, with the option to revert to global review.

The start of the reference list for the EMTCT validation criteria document, citing mainly WHO guidelines on HIV, hepatitis and syphilis, the 2030 Agenda and the 2021 UN political declaration on HIV and AIDS.

Continues the reference list, citing WHO governance guidance for EMTCT validation, UNAIDS global AIDS updates, WHO antiretroviral guidelines, research on maternal syphilis outcomes and a policy brief on dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests.

Continues the reference list, citing work on congenital syphilis burden, WHO's hepatitis B vaccine position paper, principles of disease elimination and WHO pages on other elimination efforts such as leprosy, onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, dracunculiasis and neonatal tetanus.

Continues the reference list, citing WHO guidance on HIV and infant feeding, the UNAIDS Global Plan towards eliminating new HIV infections in children, Spectrum modelling, congenital syphilis strategy and regional hepatitis plans.

Continues the reference list, citing the Global Vaccine Action Plan, Immunization Agenda 2030, immunization coverage estimates, WHO hepatitis strategic information and prevention guidelines, and international guidelines on HIV and human rights.
Continues the reference list, citing sources on human rights and gender equality in HIV, community engagement, Gavi's vaccine investment strategy, delivery care coverage and hepatitis B serosurveys.
Ends the reference list with studies on hepatitis B control in Pacific island countries and the Spectrum modelling software.

Opens Annex 1 on clinical follow-up of infants and young children exposed to HIV, syphilis or hepatitis B, noting that HIV diagnosis in infants is complicated by assay limits, ongoing exposure and maternal antibodies, so follow-up must continue until final status is known.

Presents WHO's simplified infant HIV diagnosis algorithm, with nucleic acid testing at set ages, prompt antiretroviral therapy with confirmatory retesting, and antibody testing at 18 months or three months after breastfeeding stops. The footnotes explain retesting to avoid false positives, extra testing for never-breastfed children and the continuing risk while breastfeeding lasts.

Sets out points on ruling out HIV in exposed infants, the role of nucleic acid testing and the need for high infant testing coverage, suggesting over 95% in small, low-prevalence countries and over 80% in high-prevalence ones. It also covers follow-up of syphilis-exposed infants and of hepatitis B-exposed infants, including post-vaccination serological testing as an extra indicator where only targeted birth-dose vaccination is given.

Explains WHO advice to do post-vaccination serological testing one to two months after the last hepatitis B dose, noting it is not routinely needed but is useful in elimination contexts. It describes follow-up for infants who are infected, uninfected and protected, or uninfected but non-responders needing revaccination.

Opens Annex 2 on measuring indicators for validating elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B, recommending national serosurveys of HBsAg prevalence in children aged five and under as the gold standard. It discusses the trade-offs of different age ranges and options to reduce cost, such as targeting higher-prevalence groups or multiphase survey designs.

Adds the option of integrating hepatitis B testing into existing national surveys and notes that small Pacific island countries can use a finite population correction when sizing serosurveys. It then describes measuring a mother-to-child transmission rate of 2% or less through follow-up of exposed infants in settings with targeted birth-dose vaccination, which requires strong data systems.

Explains that mathematical modelling can complement, but not replace, empirical data in judging whether hepatitis B elimination targets are met, and should use independent, peer-reviewed models. It lists uses such as setting country-specific coverage targets, designing biomarker surveys and converting prevalence into incidence estimates, noting standards comparable to Spectrum for HIV are still to be set.

Lists the web annexes of the EMTCT validation guidance to be published in 2022, including assessment checklists, report templates, data, laboratory and programme verification tools, and human rights and community engagement tools.
The back cover, giving contact details for the WHO Department of HIV/AIDS in Geneva.
